doc.title: Ingrid Sertso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, August 11, 2014

title: Why America undervalues jazz compared to Europe
summary: Europe honors jazz musicians while Americans pay $1500 to play; Han Bennink and the lack of art education here.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: In retrospect when you think about those times, do you have any thoughts on why this country did not recognize these people as important?

No. I have no idea. I still try to figure it out. Jazz in Europe, high art. I mean we are from Europe, but jazz musicians love to go over there. They get the best hotels, there is always a room with food, wine, people are honoring them, people come for autographs. But now, if a musician from Europe wants to play here he has to pay $1500.

So now, I just went to Berlin. We did — there is this big concert for Eric Dolphy. We were one of the few people that did the last concert with him, for one night, and then he died of sugar. And Han Bennink, that famous beautiful Dutch drummer. He said, “Ingrid, I can’t go to the U.S. anymore. It was my favorite trip. I can’t pay $1,500.”
“I can’t pay” — no. “I don’t want to pay the $1500.” He probably would be able to because he’s very well known and so a little bit better off.
I think we seem to value things more if they come from somewhere else.

No there is no art education here. Don’t forget, the reason why Europeans sometimes can be so arrogant, they have culture. Their history is lots of culture. Lots of art. There’s still a fight between Germany and France. Who has the better classical musicians? Who has the better classical painters? When I met Ornette first he said, “I heard of you, you come from Europe — the best classical musicians, you should be very proud.” There is no respect for art. There is no art education here.
